title: Galaxy Cluster PLCK G165.7 (NIRCam Image)
caption: Galaxy cluster PLCK G165.7+67.0 and supernova H0pe, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: PLCK G165.7+67.0, G165, SN H0pe · constellation Ursa Major
credit: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Brenda Frye (University of Arizona), Rogier Windhorst (ASU), S. Cohen (ASU), Jordan D'Silva (UWA), Anton Koekemoer (STScI), Jake Summers (ASU)

recognition.text: NASA Webb image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Hundreds of small galaxies, white, yellow, orange and red, fill a black background, and some of them look stretched out or mirrored. A long red arc stands out near the middle. This Webb picture shows the galaxy cluster PLCK G165.7+67.0, or G165, whose gravity bends and magnifies the light of the more distant universe behind it.

Within the red arc, astronomers found the light of an exploding star, a Type Ia supernova now known as SN H0pe, appearing three times as separate points. Its light reached Webb along three paths of different lengths, so each image shows the explosion at a different moment.

That time delay gives astronomers an unusual way to work out a new value for the Hubble constant, the figure that describes how fast the universe is expanding. G165's field is known for forming stars at more than 300 solar masses per year, a trait that goes along with higher rates of supernovae.
scale: The foreground cluster lies about 3.6 billion light-years from Earth, according to NASA.

understand.summary: Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) used eight infrared filters. NASA shows F090W, F115W and F150W in blue, F200W and F277W in green, and F356W, F410M and F444W in red.
understand.eye: All of these wavelengths, from 0.9 to 4.44 microns, are infrared light that the human eye cannot see, so the colors are assigned to make the differences visible.

explore: Webb's Near-Infrared Camera observed G165 on three dates in spring 2023. The distortions seen in some of the background galaxies are another product of the cluster's gravity acting as a lens on light from far behind it.
